cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Nowadays, we use different products for personal cleanliness, laundry, dishwashing and

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: household cleaning, but this is very much a 20th-century development.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: The origins of cleanliness date back to prehistoric times.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Since water is essential for life, the earliest people lived near water and knew

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: something about its cleansing properties – at least that it rinsed mud off their hands.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: During the excavation of ancient Babylon, evidence was found that soapmaking was known as

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: early as 2800 BC.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Archaeologists discovered cylinders made of clay, with inscriptions on them saying that

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: fats were boiled with askes.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: This is a method of making soap, though there's no reference to the purpose of this

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: material.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: The early Greeks bathed for aesthetic reasons and apparently didn't use soap.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Instead, they cleaned their bodies with blocks of sand, pumice and ashes, then anointed

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: themselves with oil, and scraped off the oil and dirt with a metal instrument known as a

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: strigil. They also used oil mixed with ashes. Clothes were washed without soap in streams.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: The ancient Germans and Gauls are also credited with discovering how to make a substance

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: called 'soap', made of melted animal fat and ashes.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: They used this mixture to tint their hair red.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Soap got its name, according to an ancient Roman legend, from Mount Sapo, where animals

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: were sacrificed, leaving deposits of animal fat.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Rain washed these deposits, along with wood ashes, down into the clay soil along the

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: River Tiber.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: Women found that this mixture greatly reduced the effort required to wash their clothes.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: As Roman civilisation advance, so did bathing.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: The first of the famous Roman baths, supplied with water from their aqueducts, was built

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: around 312 BC. The baths were luxurious, and bathing became very popular.

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: And by the second century AD, the Greek physician Galen recommended soap for both

cues.speaker: OM
cues.text: medicinal and cleaning purposes.
